laudatory

/LAW-duh-tor-ee/ - the stress falls on LAW · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Laudatory means expressing praise and admiration.

The retirement toast was so laudatory that the modest coach kept checking whether someone famous had walked in behind him.

Worked Example

The yearbook's page on the drama club was purely laudatory — every production 'triumphant,' every set 'ingenious' — and the faculty adviser cut only one adjective, for space.

Laudatory describes language whose whole business is praise. It is stronger than 'favorable': a favorable report may note flaws along the way, but a laudatory one exists to admire.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

admiring: Admiring means showing warm, genuine approval — a tone as much as a judgment, and you can be admiring in complete silence. Laudatory describes the language itself: words whose whole business is praise, as in a laudatory review or citation. Admiring is the feeling; laudatory is the wording.

complimentary: Complimentary remarks offer compliments, sometimes only out of politeness — a host calling every dish delicious. Laudatory language goes further and means it: praise is its whole purpose, not social smoothing. A complimentary aside flatters the moment; a laudatory citation honors a record.

approving: Approving signals agreement or acceptance, and it runs cooler than praise — a nod, a signed-off report. Laudatory language does not merely accept; it admires out loud. A committee can be approving without one warm word, while a laudatory introduction is warm from first line to last.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

scornful: expressing open contempt

withering: so harshly critical it shrivels its target

Where it sits · how heavily the praise is poured on — favorable → laudatory → gushing

favorable vs. laudatory: A favorable review leans positive but may still note flaws; it stops short of laudatory, which is praise through and through.

gushing vs. laudatory: Gushing goes further than laudatory, into excess — praise so unmeasured it starts to embarrass everyone, including its subject.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — laudat-

Root — laudat-: praised (Latin laudare, 'to praise')

Suffix — -ory

Suffix — -ory: characterized by, expressing

Put it together

Put it together: Latin laudare means 'to praise,' and its participle stem laudat- plus -ory ('expressing') builds an adjective for language that praises. The bare root still surfaces in English: critics laud a performance, and a laudable effort is one deserving praise. (Applaud, despite the sound, is a different root — plaudere, 'to clap.')

Use the root in a new word: laud

Use the root in a new word: laud: Reviewers lauded the debut for its patient, unshowy prose.

Word Choice

formal / written

Laudatory is a reviewer's and reporter's word — apply it to the words of praise (a laudatory review, citation, introduction), not to the praiseworthy thing itself; that is 'laudable.' Keep it apart from this unit's toady, too: laudatory praise can be entirely sincere, while a toady's flattery is praise with an angle.
